Built in 1961, Africa Hall holds Afewerk Tekle’s best-known work, the stained-glass triptych Total Liberation of Africa.
The square’s name is a date, 27 Miyazya, the 5 May on which Addis Ababa was freed in 1941; the monument in the middle celebrates the liberation.
Built for Haile Selassie in the 1930s, the Paradise of Princes was the scene of the failed coup of 1960.
Finished in 1942 after the liberation from Italian occupation, the cathedral holds, in its north transept, the tombs of Haile Selassie and Empress Menen.
The Gebbi, seat of Ethiopia’s emperors, keeps the mausoleum of Menelik II, of Empress Taytu and of his daughter Empress Zewditu.
The square takes its name from Meskel, the feast of the finding of the True Cross, when a great bonfire is lit here.
Among the museum’s fossils are Lucy, a partial skeleton of Australopithecus afarensis, and Selam, found between 2000 and 2004.
Built in 1955 for the silver jubilee of Haile Selassie, the palace was his home until the coup of 1974, when he was deposed here.
Opened in 2010, the museum remembers the victims of the Red Terror under the Derg, with their skulls, bones and photographs.
Built to celebrate the victory over the Italians at Adwa, in 1896, this octagonal cathedral is where Haile Selassie was crowned.
Founded by Empress Taytu, Menelik II’s wife, to lodge foreign guests, this is the oldest hotel in Addis Ababa.
The obelisk remembers the massacre that Italian forces began on Yekatit 12, 19 February 1937.
Built over the tomb of the Sufi saint Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi, the mosque in its present form is the work of Italian architects.
Designed by the Norwegian firm Snøhetta near the site of the ancient Library, the new one has shelves for eight million books.
Built in 1929 on Saad Zaghloul Square, facing the sea front, the Cecil Hotel welcomed guests such as Winston Churchill.
Destroyed by Napoleon’s army in 1798, the synagogue was rebuilt in 1850 on the site of one of 1354.
Excavated since 1960 with Polish archaeologists, Kom el-Dikka had Roman baths, lecture halls and a theatre.
Used for burials from the 2nd to the 4th century, the catacombs were found again in 1900, when a donkey fell into their shaft.
The museum is housed in an Italian-style palace that was once the consulate of the United States.
Despite its name, the column was raised in honour of the emperor Diocletian, where the Serapeum stood.
Sultan Qaitbay built this fort from 1477 to 1479 where the ancient Lighthouse of Alexandria had stood.
The historic seat of the Coptic popes stands, by tradition, where Mark the Evangelist founded the Church of Alexandria.
Built by Hajj Ibrahim Terbana and named after him, the mosque is in the Delta style of Ottoman Egypt.
Built by Alexandria’s Italians as a memorial to Khedive Ismail, it was later made the memorial to the navy’s unknown soldiers.
First named as a courtyard in 1389, it was home to beguines until the last of them died in 1971.
The flower market has stood on the Singel since 1862, where flowers were once sold from boats on the canal.
Pierre Cuypers, who also designed the Rijksmuseum, built the station, opened in 1889, on three artificial islands and 8,687 wooden piles.
Built as the city hall on 13,659 wooden piles, it became a royal palace for Louis Bonaparte in 1808.
The Skinny Bridge was first built in 1691, of wood and narrower than the stone bridge planned; it was opened by hand until 1994.
Amsterdam’s oldest building, consecrated in 1306; Rembrandt’s wife, Saskia, was buried here in 1642.
Rembrandt bought the house in 1639 and lived here until 1658, when it was auctioned after his bankruptcy.
A city gate turned weigh house in 1617; the surgeons’ guild upstairs commissioned Rembrandt’s Anatomy Lesson of Dr Tulp.
Its 87-metre tower is the tallest church tower in Amsterdam; Rembrandt was buried here in 1669, in a grave now lost.
Aosta was Augusta Praetoria, a Roman town founded in 25 BC; its Arch of Augustus still stands.
Assisi is Francis’s town: his tomb lies beneath the basilica that bears his name.
In Astorga stands the Episcopal Palace designed by Antoni Gaudí.
Raised by Phibun’s government, the monument recalls the revolution of 1932, which gave Siam a constitution.
In front of Wat Suthat, the swing served a Brahmin ceremony until 1935, when accidents brought it to an end.
This artificial hill, crowned by a golden chedi, rose where a huge chedi begun under Rama III sank into the soft ground.
Its name means milled rice, once sold here; since the 1980s it has been the backpackers’ street.
Rama III built this temple in 1846 for his granddaughter; it is known for the Loha Prasat, the Iron Palace.
Opened in 1932 for the 150th year of the Chakri dynasty, the bridge crosses to Thonburi; its middle once lifted for ships.
Founded by King Chulalongkorn in 1874, the museum fills the Front Palace of the old vice-kings, the Wang Na.
Phra Sumen is one of the few left of the fourteen forts that guarded Bangkok’s old walls.
The Temple of Dawn kept the Emerald Buddha before it crossed the river; its prang is covered in pieces of Chinese porcelain.
Older than Bangkok, when it was called Wat Salak, the temple now holds a Buddhist university for monks.
Its reclining Buddha is 46 metres long, and the temple is a home of traditional Thai massage.
In the grounds of the Grand Palace, this is the temple of the Emerald Buddha, the kings’ own.
In Barcelos, the legend goes, a roast cock stood up and crowed to save a pilgrim condemned to hang.
Just behind the Drum Tower, the Bell Tower kept the city’s official time with it until 1924.
Past the Imperial Garden, you leave the Forbidden City by its north gate, first named for the Black Tortoise of the north.
First built in 1272, under the Yuan, the Drum Tower was rebuilt here under the Ming.
From the Yongzheng Emperor on, the Qing hid the name of their heir behind the tablet above this throne.
In 1644, as rebels took Beijing, the last Ming emperor, Chongzhen, hanged himself from a tree on this hill.
Built as the home of Prince Yong, the future Yongzheng Emperor, it became a monastery of Tibetan Buddhism’s Gelug school in 1744.
Through the Meridian Gate, its south gate, you enter the Forbidden City, home of the emperors from 1420 until 1924.
Nearly 800 metres long, this hutong took its present name under the Qing, by about 1750.
Built in 1756, this screen wall has nine dragons on each side.
Built for Heshen, a minister of the Qianlong Emperor, the mansion later became the home of Prince Gong, whose name it keeps.
Shichahai’s three lakes were once part of the Grand Canal, which reached Beijing from Hangzhou.
The palace’s largest hall, on a terrace of three marble tiers, is where the Ming and Qing emperors were enthroned.
Called Chengtianmen under the Ming, this gate of the Imperial City now appears on China’s national emblem.
The square lies where the Ming and the Qing had their Corridor of a Thousand Steps; it was widened in the 1950s.
Raised in 1651, the White Dagoba crowns Jade Flower Island, in the middle of Beihai’s lake.
On 10 May 1933 books were burned here; a glass pane in the square looks down on empty shelves.
Napoleon carried the Quadriga on top of the gate off to Paris in 1806; it came back in 1814.
Finished in 1905 for Emperor William II, it holds the tombs of the Hohenzollern, Prussia’s ruling house.
In October 1961, Soviet and American tanks faced each other at this crossing, ready to fire.
Two domed churches, the French and the German, flank the concert hall Schinkel built in 1821.
Eight courtyards open one into the next behind a single gateway; they opened in 1906.
Peter Eisenman’s field of 2,711 concrete slabs was opened in 2005.
Inaugurated in 1866 with about 3,000 seats, it was the largest synagogue in Berlin.
Once one of the busiest squares in Europe, it lay empty along the Wall until 1989.
The Bundestag has sat here since 1999, under a glass dome open to visitors.
Built by East Germany between 1965 and 1969, at 368 metres it is the tallest structure in Germany.
It first stood before the Reichstag; in 1939 it was moved here, to the Großer Stern.
Here the houses stood in the East and the pavement in the West: in 1961 people jumped from their windows to flee.
The way begins in Piazza Maggiore, the heart of Bologna since the Middle Ages.
Bolsena lies on the largest volcanic lake in Europe.
The Grand Splendid theatre of 1919 is now a bookshop, with tables on its old stage.
Its design follows Dante’s Divine Comedy: 100 metres tall, one for each canto.
Founded in 1895, the national museum of fine arts now fills an old waterworks pump house.
The colonial town hall, begun in 1725, is now the museum of the May Revolution of 1810.
The president’s palace takes its name from its pink colour.
General José de San Martín, hero of independence, rests in a mausoleum inside the cathedral.
A survey of conductors by Leo Beranek ranked its hall the best in the world for opera.
Designed by Vittorio Meano, the Congress palace was inaugurated in 1906.
Eduardo Catalano’s metal flower, 23 metres tall, was made to close its six petals at night.
Raised in 1936, it marks four hundred years since the city’s first founding.
The square is named after General San Martín, whose equestrian statue stands here.
Opened in 1822, the cemetery holds the tombs of presidents and of Eva Perón.
Opened in 1858, the café counted Jorge Luis Borges among its regulars.
Burgos cathedral, begun in 1221, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Begun in 1863 and inaugurated in 1874 on land of Abdeen Bey, whose name it keeps, the palace replaced the Citadel as the seat of power.
Built by the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli when he founded Cairo, the mosque is the seat of Al-Azhar University.
Sultan al-Ghuri built his mosque and his mausoleum face to face across the street, but after the battle of Marj Dabiq, in 1516, his body was never found.
Begun in 990 and finished in 1013 by the caliph al-Hakim, whose name it bears, the mosque was restored in 1980 by the Dawoodi Bohras.
Built in 1125 under the Fatimids, it was one of Cairo’s first mosques whose façade follows the street, while its inside faces Mecca.
The Gate of Victory, built by the vizier Badr al-Jamali in 1087, has names of Napoleon’s officers carved near its top.
The southern gate of the Fatimid walls, built in 1092, bears on its towers the two minarets of the mosque of al-Mu’ayyad, added in the 15th century.
Finished in 1347 for the emir Aqsunqur, it is called the Blue Mosque for the tiles a Janissary, Ibrahim Agha, added in the 17th century.
Opened on Tahrir Square in 1902, the museum keeps in its garden the tomb of Auguste Mariette, its first curator.
Its collection began in the ruined mosque of al-Hakim, further on; this neo-Mamluk building was finished in 1902.
The bazaar is named after a caravanserai built by the emir Jaharkas al-Khalili; Naguib Mahfouz set Midaq Alley here.
In Saladin’s Citadel, Muhammad Ali’s mosque holds his tomb and a clock sent by the King of the French in return for the obelisk of Luxor, now in Paris.
Sultan Qalawun’s hospital, madrasa and mausoleum date from 1284 and 1285; the complex is said to have been built in just thirteen months.
Begun by Sultan Hasan in 1356, the madrasa taught the four schools of Sunni law, each, it is said, in one of the great iwans around its courtyard.
The statue in the middle of the square is of Talaat Harb, who founded Banque Misr in 1920.
Caldas de Reis grew around hot springs that the Romans already used.
Held to be South Africa’s oldest mosque, from 1794, it had as its first imam Tuan Guru, who had written out the Qur’an from memory in prison.
Bo-Kaap, Afrikaans for above the Cape, is the old Malay Quarter on the slopes of Signal Hill, known for its brightly painted houses.
Its first stone laid in 1666, the Dutch East India Company’s fort has five bastions named after the titles of the Prince of Orange.
Hours after his release, on 11 February 1990, Nelson Mandela made his first public speech from this balcony; a statue of him has stood there since 2018.
Laid out by the first European settlers to grow fresh food for ships rounding the Cape, the garden keeps South Africa’s oldest cultivated pear tree, from about 1652.
Opened in 1994, the museum remembers the 60,000 people forced to leave District Six under apartheid, in the 1970s.
This district was built on land won from Table Bay in the 1930s and 1940s: the Castle, ahead, once stood on the shore.
Laid out in 1696, the square was a slave market and a vegetable market; the front of its Old Town House is held to be the city’s historic centre.
First lit in 1824, South Africa’s oldest lighthouse has had a foghorn since 1926.
Its four statues are South Africa’s Nobel Peace Prize winners, Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, F. W. de Klerk and Nelson Mandela, with Table Mountain behind them.
Built by the Dutch East India Company in 1679 to house the people it enslaved, the lodge served as such until 1811.
Founded in 1825, the museum has stood in the Company’s Garden since 1897; among its collections are whale skeletons.
Begun in 1901 to Herbert Baker’s design, the cathedral holds the remains of Archbishop Desmond Tutu, before its high altar.
Built for the 2010 football World Cup, the stadium hosted one of its quarter-finals and a semi-final.
Its two basins are named after Queen Victoria and her son Prince Alfred, who began the harbour’s breakwater in 1860.
Twenty-three vaults in the walls, built as storerooms and later used as prison cells.
In 1586, still unfinished, the cathedral was damaged in Francis Drake’s attack on the city.
This palace, finished in 1770, was the seat of the Inquisition’s tribunal in Cartagena.
Begun in 1614, the walls were built in stages to protect the city from pirates.
In 1741 its defenders, under Blas de Lezo, held off the British fleet of Admiral Vernon.
The church of Santo Domingo, on this square, was built between about 1565 and 1630.
The main gate of the walled city takes its name from the clock set on it in the 18th century.
On 11 November 1811 the people of Getsemaní, with Pedro Romero, pushed Cartagena to declare its independence.
At the iron cross, about 1,500 metres up, pilgrims leave a stone brought from home.
In its Last Supper, attributed to Marcos Zapata, a guinea pig is on the table.
The Jesuits built their church on Amarucancha, the palace of the Inca Huayna Capac.
The white Christ, eight metres tall, was a gift to the city from its Palestinian Christians, in 1945.
This was the heart of the Inca capital; the City of Cusco has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1983.
Its Quechua name, Kusipata, means the place of joy; it was part of the great Inca square.
An Inca huaca, a sacred place carved into the rock, with a shrine hollowed out beneath it.
The Incas’ Temple of the Sun, once lined with gold; the Dominican convent was built on its walls.
Its largest stone weighs over a hundred tonnes; the Inti Raymi, the Inca feast of the sun, is held nearby every 24 June.
The church of San Blas keeps a pulpit carved in cedar, a marvel of Churrigueresque woodwork.
Paullu Inca, brother of Atahualpa, founded this church; his remains were found beneath it in 2007.
Cusco’s central market since 1925, declared part of Peru’s cultural heritage in 2024, it sells fruit, meat and cooked food.
In Hatun Rumiyoc street, the stone of twelve angles is set in the wall of an Inca palace.
Imagined by Léopold Sédar Senghor, the museum tells the histories and cultures of Black people everywhere.
Seat of the archbishop of Dakar, the cathedral was consecrated by Cardinal Jean Verdier, archbishop of Paris.
Built by Moroccan and French architects, the Grand Mosque was inaugurated in 1964 by King Hassan II of Morocco and President Senghor.
Renovated for the 2026 Youth Olympic Games, the stadium is used by two of Dakar’s football clubs, ASC Jaraaf and US Gorée.
Part of the IFAN institute, the museum of African art has borne the name of the naturalist Théodore Monod since 2007.
The Médina was founded by the French colonial authorities in 1914; the singer Youssou N’Dour was born here.
Senegal’s single chamber, the National Assembly, sits here; it twice had a Senate beside it, from 1999 to 2001 and from 2007 to 2012.
Ordered in 1902 for the governor-general of French West Africa, who until then lived in Saint-Louis, the palace is now the home of Senegal’s president.
Opened in 1965, Senegal’s national theatre is named after the French-Senegalese actor Daniel Sorano.
On the Corniche, beside the Médina, Soumbédioune’s craft market is one of the best known in Dakar.
In front of the station stand Demba and Dupont, a Senegalese tirailleur and a French soldier, statues unveiled in 1923.
Grown from a medical school of French West Africa, the university bears the name of the historian Cheikh Anta Diop.
Founded in 859 and 860 by Maryam al-Fihri, Fatima’s sister, the mosque is known for its tall north gate of zellij and carved wood.
Built from 1350 to 1355 for the Marinid sultan Abu Inan, the madrasa was also a Friday mosque, with its own minaret; a water clock stands beside it.
Hides are softened in the white vats and dyed in the coloured ones; local tradition dates the tannery back to the founding of Fez.
Laid out by Sultan Hassan I between Fez’s two old cities, the gardens were reserved for the royal elite until 1917.
Moved here under the Marinids, Fez’s Jewish quarter was the first in Morocco to be called a mellah, perhaps after a salt store or a salty spring.
The shrine holds the tomb of the Idrisid ruler Idris II, found again around 1437; Moulay Ismail later gave it its pyramidal roof.
Founded as a mosque by Fatima al-Fihri, of a family from Kairouan, al-Qarawiyyin is cited by UNESCO as the oldest university still at work.
The royal palace covers 80 hectares; its great ornate doors on the Place des Alaouites were made in the 20th century.
Fiesole is older than Florence: the Etruscans founded it, and its Roman theatre still holds summer shows.
The way ends in Piazza della Signoria, in front of Palazzo Vecchio.
Travellers have found a hospice at this pass since about 1050, when Bernard of Aosta founded it.
In Gubbio, the Fioretti tell, Francis tamed the wolf that frightened the town.
Built by the French in place of two older markets, it was nearly destroyed by fire in 1994.
Built by the French colonial government, the prison later held American prisoners of war, who called it the Hanoi Hilton; part of it is now a museum.
Here, the legend says, Emperor Lê Lợi gave his magic sword back to a turtle, after he had driven out the Chinese.
Built by Daydé & Pillé of Paris and first named after Paul Doumer, the bridge carries the railway over the Red River.
The Thê Húc bridge leads to this temple on its islet, which honours, among others, the national hero Trần Hưng Đạo.
Known as the 36 streets, the Old Quarter once gave each street its own trade.
Finished in 1886 in the Gothic Revival style, the cathedral is said to resemble Notre-Dame de Paris.
Founded in 1070 for Confucius, the temple keeps stelae on stone turtles with the names of the scholars who passed the royal exams.
Built in 1777, it was the city’s first promenade.
A replica diamond set in the floor of its hall marks kilometre zero of Cuba’s roads.
Columbus’s remains lay in this cathedral until 1898, when they were taken to Seville.
Inaugurated in 1914, it stands where the Teatro Tacón stood before it.
From 1630 a heavy chain stretched from this castle to El Morro guarded the bay.
This is the oldest square in Old Havana.
Laid out in 1559, it was first called the Plaza Nueva, the New Square.
Bronze lions guard this promenade, which runs down to the Malecón.
One of the oldest stone forts in the Americas, it wears the Giraldilla weathervane on its tower.
The basilica on this square, begun in 1548, is now a concert hall.
Designed by I. M. Pei, it was the tallest building in Hong Kong and in Asia when it opened in 1990.
Built in 1846 for the commander of the British forces, the house is now a museum of tea ware.
A gilded bauhinia six metres tall marks the handover of Hong Kong in 1997; the flag is raised here every morning at eight.
Opened in 1986, the bank’s tower shows its steel frame outside; the bronze lions at its door follow those of its Shanghai office.
The temple honours Man Cheong, god of literature, and Kwan Tai, god of war; the Tung Wah hospitals have run it since 1908.
Every day at noon Jardines fires this gun, in amends, the story goes, for a salute once fired for the firm’s own head.
Built by the people of Wan Chai in 1863, the temple keeps a statue of Pak Tai three metres tall.
Opened in 1888, the funicular climbs from here to Victoria Peak.
Once quarters for married policemen, on the site of Queen’s College, the buildings became a creative centre in 2014.
Hong Kong’s oldest Western church, finished in 1849, stands on the only freehold land in the city.
From here the Star Ferry crosses the harbour to Tsim Sha Tsui, a service begun by Dorabjee Naorojee Mithaiwala, a Parsi.
Named for Queen Victoria’s statue, now in Victoria Park, the square keeps a single statue, of the banker Sir Thomas Jackson.
The old Central Police Station, with the magistracy and Victoria Prison, reopened to the public in 2018 as Tai Kwun.
Opened in 1957 on land reclaimed from the old Causeway Bay typhoon shelter, the park is named after Queen Victoria.
Built in 1906, this was the north block of the old Western Market.
Ivrea’s carnival is known for its battle of the oranges.
Gion is one of Japan’s best-known geisha districts; in Kyoto the geisha are called geiko.
This Zen temple was founded in 1202, with the monk Eisai as its first abbot.
The temple’s great wooden stage, built without a single nail, gave Japan the saying: to jump off the stage at Kiyomizu, to take the plunge.
Toyotomi Hideyoshi’s widow, become the nun Kōdai-in, founded this temple to pray for his soul.
Kyoto’s best-known park for the cherry blossom is famous for its great weeping cherry.
Called Kyoto’s kitchen, the market grew from fish shops that kept their fish fresh in the cold groundwater, for the palace.
This narrow lane by the Kamo River may take its name from Portuguese, and is one of Kyoto’s geisha districts.
On the way up to Kiyomizu, this stepped lane is a protected district of traditional houses.
The five-storey pagoda standing today was rebuilt in 1440, after it had been destroyed more than once.
Dedicated to the god Susanoo, the shrine holds the Gion Matsuri every July.
Francis received the stigmata at La Verna in 1224, his first biographers wrote.
León cathedral holds nearly 1,800 square metres of medieval stained glass.
Laid out in 1611, the avenue copies the Alameda de Hércules of Seville.
Lima’s Chinatown made the chifas famous, as Peru calls its Chinese restaurants.
Built for Jerónimo de Aliaga in 1536, it has been home to the same family for seventeen generations.
Pizarro laid its first stone in 1535; the cathedral took its present form between 1602 and 1797.
The president’s palace stands on the plot Pizarro kept for his own house when he founded the city.
The street joins Lima’s two great squares, in a historic centre that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The museum is in the Palacio de la Exposición, built for Lima’s International Exhibition of 1872.
The park keeps a stretch of the walls built against pirates in the 1680s, which never saw a battle.
Opened in 1939, it was modelled on the Palace of Justice in Brussels.
Named for the reservists who defended Lima in the War of the Pacific, at San Juan and Miraflores.
Francisco Pizarro founded Lima on this square on 18 January 1535, as the City of the Kings.
Opened on 27 July 1921 for the centenary of independence, it honours the liberator José de San Martín.
Built in 1610, after a flood of the Rímac had carried away the bridge before it.
Its catacombs were the city’s cemetery in colonial times; the convent is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, grew out of the lessons first given in this convent.
Almost every English and British monarch since 1066 has been crowned here.
The monarch’s London home since Queen Victoria moved in, in 1837.
Number 10 has been the Prime Minister’s house since Robert Walpole moved in, in 1735.
The wheel, 135 metres tall, opened in 2000.
It was built for the Festival of Britain, in 1951.
A rebuilding of Shakespeare’s theatre, opened in 1997 near the site of the first.
Every June the King’s birthday parade, Trooping the Colour, is held here.
Opened in June 2000, it swayed under the walkers’ feet and was closed two days later.
Its 61 metres are its distance from the bakery in Pudding Lane where the Great Fire began.
Big Ben is the great bell inside the clock tower, named Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
Pelicans have lived here since a Russian ambassador gave them to Charles II in 1664.
Christopher Wren built the cathedral after the Great Fire of 1666.
A power station until 1981, it opened as a gallery of modern art in 2000.
Founded by William the Conqueror, it keeps the Crown Jewels.
Its two halves still lift to let tall ships through, as they have since 1894.
Nelson’s Column, about 52 metres tall, remembers the battle of Trafalgar of 1805.
Wordsworth wrote a sonnet on this bridge in 1802: earth has not anything to show more fair.
Lucca’s Renaissance walls, over four kilometres around, are a park on top.
Built within the temple, the mosque holds the tomb of the sheikh Yusuf Abu al-Haggag, after whom it is named.
Lined with sphinxes, some with the heads of rams, this avenue joined the temples of Luxor and Karnak.
Built and rebuilt over some two thousand years, Karnak was the main temple of Amun, at the head of the Theban triad.
The museum is given to the ancient art of mummification, practised not only on people but on many animals.
Opened in 1975, the museum shows statues found in a cache beneath Luxor Temple, and a rebuilt wall of Akhenaten’s temple at Karnak.
The precinct of the goddess Mut, south of Karnak, keeps a sacred lake around her temple.
Of the two obelisks Ramesses II raised here, one now stands in Paris; the clock France gave in return is in Cairo’s Citadel.
Built by Ramesses III on the site of an earlier temple, this is an almost complete temple of the New Kingdom.
Beyond the village the way follows stretches of the Flaminia Militare, a road the Romans opened in 187 BC.
Begun in 1883, the cathedral was consecrated by Pope John Paul II in 1993.
Ricardo Bellver’s statue shows Lucifer at the moment of his fall from heaven.
